arXiv:2606.27780v1 [cs.AI] 26 Jun 2026

Understanding Rollout Error in Graph World Models

Xinyuan Song Affiliation: Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA Email: xinyuan.song@emory.edu    Zekun Cai Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan Affiliation: LocationMind, Tokyo, Japan Email: caizekun@csis.u-tokyo.ac.jp
Abstract

World models are often used for planning by rolling learned dynamics forward. Many planning environments, however, are not vectors or images; they are graphs of agents, tools, skills, routes, and dependencies. In these settings, a local prediction error may stay local or spread through the graph, and the failure mode changes again when edges are predicted rather than fixed. This paper studies long-horizon rollout error in Graph World Models (GWMs). We formulate a unified fixed-edge and dynamic-edge GWM framework with action nodes for node-, edge-, and graph-level decisions. We develop graph-valued rollout bounds that separate topology-induced amplification from model-induced amplification, and we introduce a joint node-edge operator for dynamic-edge rollouts. Guided by the analysis, we propose Error-Aware GWM, which combines spectral regularization, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting. Across synthetic topologies and heterogeneous agent-graph testbeds, rollout error and planning regret grow with horizon, dynamic-edge training is needed when structure evolves, and Error-Aware GWM prevents long-horizon divergence while preserving prediction accuracy. Real-world graph benchmarks clarify the scope of GWMs: they are most useful for dynamic graph rollout and agent planning, while specialized graph models remain strong on static or sparse prediction tasks. An anonymized implementation and benchmark suite will be released with the submission. Code is available at https://github.com/Hik289/graph_world_model_accumulative_error.git.

1 Introduction

A world model Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) represents environment observations as states and predicts future states conditioned on actions. Modern world models trained on large-scale data Hafner et al. (2018); Hafner et al. (2020); Hafner et al. (2023); Chua et al. (2018); Wu et al. (2024); Bruce et al. (2024) have shown strong planning, prediction, and generation capabilities. Most of them, however, are built for vector- or image-like states. They do not directly capture environments whose state is a graph. Such environments are common in agent planning: multi-agent calling trees coordinate distributed task execution Anokhin et al. (2024), skill graphs encode tool dependencies, and communication networks route actions among interacting entities. Planning in these settings requires reasoning about node states and about how effects travel through relations. The same autoregressive rollout that enables long-horizon planning also creates a risk: prediction errors can compound and degrade downstream decisions Asadi et al. (2018); Janner et al. (2019).

Graph World Models (GWMs) address this setting by autoregressively predicting graph states Gt=(V,Et,Xt,At)G_{t}=(V,E_{t},X_{t},A_{t}) Feng et al. (2025). Given a learned transition model ℱθ​(G^k,ak)\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k}), a GWM rolls out G^1,…,G^H\hat{G}_{1},\ldots,\hat{G}_{H} and scores candidate action sequences. Existing work has mostly studied graph foundation models for static graph tasks Liu et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024) or domain-specific graph planning Zhang et al. (2021); Ammanabrolu and Riedl (2021). Feng et al. Feng et al. (2025) introduced a unified GWM with action nodes, but their setting focuses on fixed-edge (FE) environments. It remains unclear how GWMs behave under long-horizon rollout error and in dynamic-edge (DE) regimes.

Graph structure makes compounding error harder to analyze than in vector-state world models. In vector settings, rollout error is often summarized by a scalar Lipschitz constant. In graph settings, the same local error can behave very differently depending on topology. An error on a chain may stay localized; an error on a hub, dense graph, or high-spectral-radius topology can spread widely, consistent with spectral analyses of graph propagation, graph-network dynamics, and GNN stability Battaglia et al. (2016); Battaglia et al. (2018); Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. (2018); Oono and Suzuki (2020); Chamberlain et al. (2021). The problem is harder when edges are predicted. A node-state error can corrupt future edge prediction, and an edge error can change later message passing. GWM rollout error is therefore not just scalar prediction error; it is a topology-dependent, and sometimes coupled, node-edge dynamical process.

Existing rollout-error theory is not designed for graph-structured planning. Standard model-based RL analyses bound compounding error with a scalar Lipschitz constant over a fixed-dimensional state vector Asadi et al. (2018); Janner et al. (2019). This misses three aspects of graph rollouts. First, topology is explicit: for a message-passing GWM, node-error growth separates into a topology term ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) and a model term ∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}, where AA is the adjacency matrix, ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) is its spectral radius, and WℓW_{\ell} are layer weights. Second, dynamic graphs require coupled error dynamics: node-feature error ekX=‖X^k−Xk‖Fe^{X}_{k}=\|\hat{X}_{k}-X_{k}\|_{F} and edge error ekA=‖A^k−Ak‖Fe^{A}_{k}=\|\hat{A}_{k}-A_{k}\|_{F} evolve together rather than through a scalar recursion. Third, rollout error must be tied to planning regret over horizon HH. These gaps motivate our graph-valued analysis, which replaces the scalar constant with GEAF^=ρ⁡(A)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}=\rho(A)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2} and uses a joint node-edge operator BB for the recursion of (ekX,ekA)(e^{X}_{k},e^{A}_{k}) in dynamic-edge GWMs.

We analyze accumulative rollout error in GWMs both theoretically and empirically. The graph error amplification factor GEAF^=ρ⁡(A)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}=\rho(A)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2} separates topology-dependent amplification from the model-dependent spectral norm product. For dynamic-edge GWMs, we introduce a joint node-edge error operator BB that captures node-to-node, edge-to-node, node-to-edge, and edge-to-edge propagation. This operator cleanly separates two regimes: fixed-edge (FE) models have no edge-prediction head, so MX=0M_{X}=0 and the dynamics reduce to node-only prediction; dynamic-edge (DE) models have an edge-prediction head, so MX>0M_{X}>0 and node-edge cross-coupling becomes active.

We evaluate the framework on a seven-topology synthetic benchmark with existing GWM baselines, including GCN Kipf and Welling (2017), MPNN Gilmer et al. (2017), GPS Rampášek et al. (2022), and ActionNode GWM Feng et al. (2025). The benchmark includes FE and DE simulators, plus heterogeneous agent-graph testbeds. The results support a regime-dependent view of GWM rollout error. Long rollouts turn small prediction errors into larger planning errors. When graph structure evolves, dynamic-edge training sharply outperforms fixed-edge training, and the learned dynamics exhibit the node-edge coupling predicted by the joint operator. The central empirical point is that GWM stability is not an architecture property alone; it depends on topology, horizon, and rollout regime.

We further propose Error-Aware GWM to improve rollout stability on high-spectral-radius graphs. It combines spectral regularization, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting to control topology-induced amplification while preserving prediction accuracy. Empirically, Error-Aware GWM removes the divergence observed in vanilla GCN rollouts and keeps long-horizon prediction error low. Simpler stabilizers can reduce divergence, but often lose predictive fidelity. This distinction matters: a useful graph world model must be stable enough to roll out and accurate enough for those rollouts to support planning.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Unified GWM framework with FE/DE instantiations (Section 3). We formulate graph-structured agent planning as state-action-transition modeling and support both fixed-edge and dynamic-edge rollouts.

  • •

    Topology-aware rollout error theory (Section 4). We develop graph-valued error bounds that account for topology-dependent amplification and node-edge coupling during autoregressive rollout.

  • •

    Error-Aware GWM for stable planning (Section 6). We introduce a training objective that combines spectral control, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting to improve long-horizon stability.

  • •

    Evaluation across synthetic and agent-graph settings (Section 7). We test the framework across diverse graph topologies, rollout regimes, and agent-graph environments to study when GWMs are stable or unstable.

  • •

    Scope analysis on real-world benchmarks (Section 7.7.1). We evaluate GWMs beyond controlled synthetic dynamics and clarify their practical boundary relative to standard graph methods.

2 Related Work

World models for planning.

World models have been widely studied in model-based reinforcement learning, where a learned dynamics model is used to simulate future trajectories for planning or policy learning. A central challenge is compounding error: small one-step model errors can accumulate over long rollouts and degrade decision quality. Asadi et al. Asadi et al. (2018) analyze this effect through Lipschitz continuity of learned transition models. PETS uses probabilistic ensembles and trajectory sampling to propagate uncertainty during model-based planning Chua et al. (2018). Janner et al. Janner et al. (2019) study model-based policy optimization with short branched rollouts to reduce error accumulation. Kakade and Langford Kakade and Langford (2002) provide simulation-lemma-style tools that connect model error to policy performance. Recent systems reduce rollout drift through retrieval-augmented context Chen et al. (2025), hierarchical latent planning Zhang et al. (2026), uncertainty-based rollout truncation Ni et al. (2025), modular dynamics experts Li et al. (2025a), skill-level abstraction Gürtler and Martius (2025), scheduled-sampling-style training Rivard et al. (2025), and controlled long-horizon evaluation benchmarks Li et al. (2025b). These works motivate rollout-error analysis, but they do not model graph topology, message passing, or coupled node-edge prediction.

Graph neural networks and graph-structured prediction.

Graph neural networks provide a standard framework for learning over graph-structured data by propagating information along edges. Interaction Networks and Graph Networks introduced object- and relation-centric neural dynamics for physical reasoning Battaglia et al. (2016); Battaglia et al. (2018), and graph-network physics engines showed that such models can support inference and control in dynamical systems Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. (2018). Graph convolutional networks aggregate normalized neighborhood information Kipf and Welling (2017). Message-passing neural networks generalize local edge-based aggregation Gilmer et al. (2017). Graph transformers such as GPS combine message passing with global attention Rampášek et al. (2022). Prior theory shows that graph propagation is strongly affected by spectral properties of the adjacency or normalized adjacency matrix Oono and Suzuki (2020), while diffusion-based GNNs connect graph learning to stability of discretized diffusion dynamics Chamberlain et al. (2021). Related work on graph rewiring studies how modifying topology can improve information flow and reduce harmful propagation effects Tori et al. (2024). Physics-informed rewiring further studies topology modification for long-range interactions in graph neural networks Yu et al. (2025). These results suggest that topology can shape prediction behavior, but they mainly study representation learning or one-step dynamics rather than autoregressive graph rollouts where prediction errors become future inputs.

Graph world models.

Graph world models extend world modeling to graph-structured states. Feng et al. Feng et al. (2025) introduce a GWM framework that represents multimodal observations, graph states, action nodes, and target nodes within a unified graph interface. WorldGraph uses latent landmarks as a graph-structured abstraction for planning Zhang et al. (2021). Value Memory Graph constructs graph-structured memory for offline reinforcement learning Zhu et al. (2022). Knowledge-graph world models represent textual environments through structured relational memory Ammanabrolu and Riedl (2021). Contrastive structured world models learn object-centric relational dynamics Kipf et al. (2020). Dyn-O builds structured world models with object-centric representations Wang et al. (2025). These works mainly focus on representation, architecture, and task performance. Our work instead studies long-horizon error behavior: how topology affects rollout error, how fixed-edge and dynamic-edge regimes differ, and how node and edge prediction errors interact through a joint operator.

Agent graphs and skill-graph systems.

Multi-agent and tool-using systems increasingly organize computation as graphs, including agent calling-trees, knowledge-graph memories, tool graphs, and skill graphs. AriGraph uses graph memory for LLM agents Anokhin et al. (2024). Audited Skill-Graph Self-Improvement studies verifier-backed skill-graph maintenance Huang and Huang (2025). CASCADE studies cumulative agentic skill creation through autonomous development and evolution Huang et al. (2026). Reinforcement learning for self-improving agents with skill libraries studies policy learning over reusable skills Wang et al. (2026). GraSP compiles retrieved skills into a typed skill graph so failed subgraphs can be repaired locally rather than replanning the full trajectory Xia et al. (2026). These works show the practical value of graph-structured agent execution. Our work is complementary: we analyze how prediction errors accumulate when such graph states are rolled out over time, and we propose Error-Aware GWM to improve long-horizon stability in graph-based planning.

3 Graph World Model Framework

3.1 Preliminaries: Agent Graph World

A Graph World Model (GWM) represents an agent environment as an evolving graph and predicts future graph states for planning. At time tt, the graph state is

Gt=(V,Et,Xt,At).G_{t}=(V,E_{t},X_{t},A_{t}). (3.1)

Here, VV is the fixed set of agent, tool, skill, or task nodes; EtE_{t} is the edge set; Xt∈ℝN×dX_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} is the node-feature matrix; and At∈{0,1}N×NA_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N} is the adjacency matrix. In an agent system, node features can encode agent status, tool outputs, skill availability, task progress, or failure signals. Edges represent calling, dependency, routing, or communication relations.

An action ata_{t} is represented as an action node injected into the graph. The learned transition model

ℱθ:(Gt,at)↦G^t+1\mathcal{F}_{\theta}:(G_{t},a_{t})\mapsto\hat{G}_{t+1} (3.2)

predicts the next graph state. During planning, an agent evaluates candidate action sequences a1,…,aHa_{1},\ldots,a_{H} by rolling out

G^k+1=ℱθ(G^k,ak),k=0,…,H−1,\hat{G}_{k+1}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k}),\qquad k=0,\ldots,H-1, (3.3)

and scoring the predicted outcomes. Thus, GWM planning reduces long-horizon decision-making to simulation over predicted graph trajectories.

3.2 Action Node Mechanism

Following Feng et al. Feng et al. (2025), actions are encoded as action nodes connected to the current graph. This gives a unified representation for three kinds of planning actions: node-level actions, which modify a specific agent, skill, tool, or task node; edge-level actions, which add, remove, or update dependency or communication edges; and graph-level actions, which change global routing, coordination, or allocation patterns.

We use two action-node connection types. Explicit action nodes connect to target nodes through task-defined structure, such as a planner calling a tool or assigning a subtask to an executor. Retrieval-based action nodes connect through embedding similarity or retrieval, such as a query routed to related skill nodes or auxiliary tools. The same transition model can therefore represent explicit decisions and soft retrieval-based dependencies in one agent graph.

3.3 Two GWM Instantiations

Fixed-Edge GWM (FE-GWM).

In the fixed-edge setting, topology is fixed during rollout and only node states are predicted. A representative GCN-style transition is

X^k+1=tanh⁡(A~​X^k​W1+U​ak)​W2+ξk,\hat{X}_{k+1}=\tanh(\tilde{A}\hat{X}_{k}W_{1}+Ua_{k})W_{2}+\xi_{k}, (3.4)

where

A~=D−1/2AD−1/2.\tilde{A}=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}. (3.5)

Here, U​akUa_{k} injects the action signal and ξk\xi_{k} denotes rollout noise. This setting covers ActionNode GWM Feng et al. (2025) and standard GNN-based world models with fixed agent-graph structure. Since edges are not predicted, FE-GWM propagates node-state error through a fixed graph, with dynamics governed by ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) and the model weight norms.

Dynamic-Edge GWM (DE-GWM).

In the dynamic-edge setting, both node features and graph structure are predicted autoregressively. In addition to the node transition, DE-GWM uses an edge-prediction head such as

A^i​j=σ⁡(hi⊤​Q​hj),\hat{A}_{ij}=\sigma(h_{i}^{\top}Qh_{j}), (3.6)

where hi,hjh_{i},h_{j} are node embeddings and QQ parameterizes pairwise edge scores. The model is trained with

ℒ=ℒnode+λe​BCE​(A^,A)+12​‖W‖2​‖Q‖2.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\rm node}+\lambda_{e}\mathrm{BCE}(\hat{A},A)+\tfrac{1}{2}\|W\|_{2}\|Q\|_{2}. (3.7)

This setting models changing agent interactions, such as task routing, tool calls, validation links, or recovery paths. DE-GWM activates node-edge cross-coupling: node errors can affect future edge prediction, and edge errors can change future message passing. In the joint-operator view, FE-GWM is the special case with no edge-prediction head and MX=0M_{X}=0; DE-GWM has MX>0M_{X}>0 and enables node-edge feedback.

4 Error Amplification Theory

Framework overview.

Figures 1–3 summarize the graph rollout-error framework. Figure 1 shows topology-dependent amplification: with the same model and initial error, low-GEAF graphs keep errors more local, while high-GEAF hub-like graphs spread them faster. Figure 2 presents the autoregressive rollout pipeline and the joint node-edge error operator BB. Figure 3 contrasts FE and DE regimes, where edge prediction determines whether BB reduces to node-only dynamics or activates node-edge coupling.

4.1 Assumptions

We state the assumptions used in the analysis. They specify the graph-state domain, the one-step approximation error, the message-passing form of node prediction, the Lipschitz structure of dynamic edge prediction, and the reward conditions needed to convert rollout error into planning regret. These assumptions match our synthetic and heterogeneous agent-graph simulators: node identities are fixed during rollout, node features and adjacency matrices are bounded, and FE models are recovered when the edge-update map is absent.

Assumption 1 (Compact graph state space).

At each time tt, the graph state is Gt=(Vt,Et,Xt,At)G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t},X_{t},A_{t}) with fixed |Vt|=N|V_{t}|=N, node features Xt∈ℝN×DX_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}, and continuous adjacency matrix At∈[0,1]N×NA_{t}\in[0,1]^{N\times N}. There exist constants RX,RA<∞R_{X},R_{A}<\infty such that

‖Xt‖F≤RX,‖At‖F≤RA\|X_{t}\|_{F}\leq R_{X},\qquad\|A_{t}\|_{F}\leq R_{A} (4.1)

for all rollout steps t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

Assumption 1 holds by construction in our simulators. The main synthetic graphs, agent calling-tree testbed, and skill-graph testbed all keep node identities fixed. Bounded node features follow from bounded nonlinearities or feature clipping, and bounded adjacency follows from At∈[0,1]N×NA_{t}\in[0,1]^{N\times N}. For growing graphs, the same analysis can be extended by replacing BB with a time-varying operator BtB_{t} and assuming suptρ⁡(Bt)<∞\sup_{t}\rho(B_{t})<\infty.

Assumption 2 (Uniform one-step model error).

Let F⋆=(FX⋆,FA⋆)F^{\star}=(F^{X\star},F^{A\star}) be the true graph transition and Fθ=(FθX,FθA)F_{\theta}=(F_{\theta}^{X},F_{\theta}^{A}) be the learned GWM transition. On the compact domain in Assumption 1, there exist constants ϵX,ϵA≥0\epsilon_{X},\epsilon_{A}\geq 0 such that

∥FθX(X,A,a)−FX⋆(X,A,a)∥F\displaystyle\|F_{\theta}^{X}(X,A,a)-F^{X\star}(X,A,a)\|_{F} ≤ϵX,\displaystyle\leq\epsilon_{X}, (4.2)
∥FθA(X,A,a)−FA⋆(X,A,a)∥F\displaystyle\|F_{\theta}^{A}(X,A,a)-F^{A\star}(X,A,a)\|_{F} ≤ϵA.\displaystyle\leq\epsilon_{A}.

Assumption 2 is the graph analogue of the standard one-step model-error assumption in model-based reinforcement learning. The constants ϵX\epsilon_{X} and ϵA\epsilon_{A} are worst-case one-step node and edge prediction errors. If only expected one-step error is available, the same recursion gives an expected rollout-error bound with the same operator form.

Assumption 3 (Message-passing node transition).

The learned node update has the message-passing form

FθX​(X,A,a)=σ⁡(A^​X​W1+U​a​𝟏⊤)​W2,F_{\theta}^{X}(X,A,a)=\sigma(\hat{A}XW_{1}+Ua\mathbf{1}^{\top})W_{2}, (4.3)

where σ\sigma is coordinate-wise Lipschitz with constant Lσ≤1L_{\sigma}\leq 1, A^\hat{A} is the propagation matrix induced by AA, W1,W2W_{1},W_{2} are learnable weight matrices, and UU maps the action embedding into the node-update space.

Assumption 3 covers standard GNN-style node predictors, including GCN, MPNN-style message passing, graph transformers, and ActionNode GWM variants after choosing the propagation matrix A^\hat{A}. Multi-layer models are handled by composing layer-wise Lipschitz constants, which gives the weight product ∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}. Non-graph MLP world models are the degenerate case with no topology-dependent propagation.

Assumption 4 (Lipschitz dynamic edge update).

For DE models, the learned edge update is Lipschitz in both node features and the current adjacency. In particular, there exist constants MX,MA,LA<∞M_{X},M_{A},L_{A}<\infty such that node and edge errors satisfy the coupled bounds

ek+1X\displaystyle e^{X}_{k+1} ≤LX​ekX+LA​ekA+ϵX,\displaystyle\leq L_{X}e^{X}_{k}+L_{A}e^{A}_{k}+\epsilon_{X}, (4.4)
ek+1A\displaystyle e^{A}_{k+1} ≤MX​ekX+MA​ekA+ϵA.\displaystyle\leq M_{X}e^{X}_{k}+M_{A}e^{A}_{k}+\epsilon_{A}.

Assumption 4 captures differentiable or relaxed differentiable edge predictors, such as a bilinear edge head followed by a bounded projection. In FE models, there is no edge-prediction head, so MX=0M_{X}=0 and MA=0M_{A}=0. The joint node-edge operator then reduces to fixed-edge node-error recursion, which is the main regime distinction in our theory.

Assumption 5 (Lipschitz reward and bounded reward approximation error).

The true reward R⋆​(G,a)R^{\star}(G,a) is Lipschitz under a graph distance dGd_{G}: for all graph states G,G′G,G^{\prime} and actions aa,

|R⋆​(G,a)−R⋆​(G′,a)|≤LR​dG​(G,G′).|R^{\star}(G,a)-R^{\star}(G^{\prime},a)|\leq L_{R}d_{G}(G,G^{\prime}). (4.5)

The learned reward model RθR_{\theta} has uniformly bounded error

|Rθ​(G,a)−R⋆​(G,a)|≤ϵR.|R_{\theta}(G,a)-R^{\star}(G,a)|\leq\epsilon_{R}. (4.6)

Assumption 5 is used only to connect rollout error to planning regret. For sparse or discontinuous task rewards, the bound can be applied to a smoothed or shaped reward, with the smoothing error included in the final regret bound.

Assumption 6 (Discounted finite-horizon return).

Planning uses the finite-horizon discounted return

J⋆=∑k=0H−1γk​rt+k,γ∈[0,1].J^{\star}=\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}r_{t+k},\qquad\gamma\in[0,1]. (4.7)

Assumption 6 follows the standard finite-horizon planning setup. The case γ=1\gamma=1 is allowed for finite HH. For infinite-horizon analysis, one needs γ<1\gamma<1 and a stable enough error operator; otherwise, the regret bound correctly diverges when rollout errors are amplified over time.

Assumption 7 (Linearized graph distance).

The graph distance used in the regret analysis is bounded by a linear combination of node and edge errors:

dG​(Gk,G^k)≤α​‖Xk−X^k‖F+β​‖Ak−A^k‖F,d_{G}(G_{k},\hat{G}_{k})\leq\alpha\|X_{k}-\hat{X}_{k}\|_{F}+\beta\|A_{k}-\hat{A}_{k}\|_{F}, (4.8)

where α,β≥0\alpha,\beta\geq 0.

Assumption 7 translates the vector error recursion into a reward-error bound. It is natural when node identities are fixed across rollout steps, as in our simulators. Spectral adjacency distances and edge-set distances can be upper-bounded by Frobenius-norm edge error, so their effects can be absorbed into β\beta.

Together, Assumptions 1–7 define the scope of the theory. Lemma 1 uses compact state, one-step error, and message passing. Lemma 2 adds the dynamic-edge Lipschitz condition. Lemma 3 uses the same nonnegative operator structure with spectral norm bounds. Lemma 4 uses the reward and graph-distance assumptions to convert rollout error into planning regret.

4.2 Problem Formulation

We study how prediction errors accumulate when a GWM is rolled out for planning. The graph state GtG_{t} and transition model ℱθ\mathcal{F}_{\theta} are defined in Equations (3.1)–(3.2). Starting from an initial predicted graph G^0\hat{G}_{0}, the model generates an HH-step predicted trajectory according to Equation (3.3). Because each predicted state becomes the input to the next step, one-step errors can accumulate and affect downstream decisions.

Let (Xk,Ak)(X_{k},A_{k}) denote the true node features and adjacency at rollout step kk, and let (X^k,A^k)(\hat{X}_{k},\hat{A}_{k}) denote their GWM predictions. We measure node and edge rollout errors by

ekX=‖X^k−Xk‖F,ekA=‖A^k−Ak‖F.e^{X}_{k}=\|\hat{X}_{k}-X_{k}\|_{F},\qquad e^{A}_{k}=\|\hat{A}_{k}-A_{k}\|_{F}. (4.9)

We collect them into the joint error vector

uk=(ekX,ekA)⊤.u_{k}=(e^{X}_{k},e^{A}_{k})^{\top}. (4.10)

The central question is how uku_{k} evolves with horizon, topology, and rollout regime. In fixed-edge (FE) GWMs, the adjacency is fixed and only node states are predicted. In dynamic-edge (DE) GWMs, both node states and edges are predicted, so node and edge errors can influence each other.

Our analysis uses the assumptions stated in Section 4.1: compact graph states, bounded one-step node and edge prediction errors, a message-passing node transition, a Lipschitz dynamic edge update for DE models, and a Lipschitz reward used to translate rollout error into planning regret.

4.3 Fixed-Edge Rollout Error

We first analyze the fixed-edge (FE) regime, where topology is held fixed and only node features are predicted. Rollout error then propagates through a fixed message-passing operator. The bound separates the topology-dependent part of amplification from the model-dependent part.

Lemma 1 (Fixed-edge node error bound).

Assume fixed adjacency At≡AA_{t}\equiv A and a message-passing node transition with activation Lipschitz constant LσL_{\sigma}. Suppose the one-step node prediction error is bounded by ϵX\epsilon_{X}. Then, for any rollout step k≥0k\geq 0,

ekX\displaystyle e^{X}_{k} ≤LXk​e0X+ϵX​LXk−1LX−1,\displaystyle\leq L_{X}^{k}e^{X}_{0}+\epsilon_{X}\frac{L_{X}^{k}-1}{L_{X}-1}, (4.11)
LX\displaystyle L_{X} =Lσ​ρ⁡(A)⏟topology​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2⏟model.\displaystyle=L_{\sigma}\underbrace{\rho(A)}_{\text{topology}}\underbrace{\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}}_{\text{model}}.

Lemma 1 shows that FE-GWM rollout error is controlled by two factors. The topology factor ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) determines how strongly errors can spread through the graph. The model factor ∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2} captures layer-wise amplification induced by the learned transition model. This motivates the Graph Error Amplification Factor

GEAF^​(G)=ρ⁡(A)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2.\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)=\rho(A)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}. (4.12)

Thus, with the same model weights, different graph topologies can induce different long-horizon error growth rates. The proof of Lemma 1 is provided in Appendix A.1.

4.4 Dynamic-Edge Rollout Error

We next analyze the dynamic-edge (DE) regime, where the GWM predicts both node states and graph structure. Here, rollout errors are coupled: node-feature errors can affect future edge prediction, and edge errors can change future message passing. We capture this interaction with a joint node-edge error operator.

Lemma 2 (Joint node-edge error bound).

Assume a DE GWM with bounded one-step errors ϵX\epsilon_{X} and ϵA\epsilon_{A}. Suppose that the node and edge errors satisfy the coupled Lipschitz bounds

ek+1X\displaystyle e^{X}_{k+1} ≤LX​ekX+LA​ekA+ϵX,\displaystyle\leq L_{X}e^{X}_{k}+L_{A}e^{A}_{k}+\epsilon_{X}, (4.13)
ek+1A\displaystyle e^{A}_{k+1} ≤MX​ekX+MA​ekA+ϵA.\displaystyle\leq M_{X}e^{X}_{k}+M_{A}e^{A}_{k}+\epsilon_{A}.

Let uk=(ekX,ekA)⊤u_{k}=(e^{X}_{k},e^{A}_{k})^{\top}. Then

uk+1\displaystyle u_{k+1} ⪯B​uk+ϵ,\displaystyle\preceq Bu_{k}+\epsilon, (4.14)
B\displaystyle B =(LXLAMXMA),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}L_{X}&L_{A}\\ M_{X}&M_{A}\end{pmatrix},
ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =(ϵX,ϵA)⊤.\displaystyle=(\epsilon_{X},\epsilon_{A})^{\top}.

The spectral radius of BB is

ρ⁡(B)\displaystyle\rho(B) =12[(LX+MA)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(L_{X}+M_{A}) (4.15)
+(LX−MA)2+4​LA​MX].\displaystyle+\sqrt{(L_{X}-M_{A})^{2}+4L_{A}M_{X}}\Big].

If LA​MX>0L_{A}M_{X}>0, then

ρ⁡(B)>max⁡(LX,MA).\rho(B)>\max(L_{X},M_{A}). (4.16)

Lemma 2 shows that DE-GWM rollout error is governed by a coupled operator rather than a scalar node-error recursion. The off-diagonal terms LAL_{A} and MXM_{X} encode edge-to-node and node-to-edge error propagation. In FE models, there is no edge-prediction head, so MX=0M_{X}=0 and the recursion reduces to node-only prediction. In DE models, MX>0M_{X}>0 activates node-edge feedback, and Equation (4.16) shows that the coupled spectral radius can exceed both uncoupled components. The proof is provided in Appendix A.2.

4.5 GEAF as a Proxy for the Joint Operator

The joint operator BB captures coupled node-edge error propagation, but estimating all of its entries can be difficult. We therefore use GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} as a topology-aware proxy for the dominant rollout amplification scale.

Lemma 3 (GEAF proxy bound).

Assume the signal-dominant regime ‖A‖2≥RX\|A\|_{2}\geq R_{X}, where RXR_{X} bounds the non-topological contribution to the first-row error term. Then

ρ⁡(B)\displaystyle\rho(B) ≤GEAF^​(G)​(1+RX‖A‖2)\displaystyle\leq\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)\left(1+\frac{R_{X}}{\|A\|_{2}}\right) (4.17)
≤2​GEAF^​(G).\displaystyle\leq 2\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G).

Moreover, when model weights are fixed across topologies, the rank order of GEAF^​(G)\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G) follows the rank order of ρ⁡(A)\rho(A).

Lemma 3 shows that GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} upper-bounds the joint operator up to a constant factor in the signal-dominant regime. In FE models, MX=0M_{X}=0, so ρ⁡(B)=LX=GEAF^\rho(B)=L_{X}=\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} by construction; this is an identity rather than empirical validation. In DE models, MX>0M_{X}>0 breaks this identity, so comparing ρ⁡(B)\rho(B) and GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} becomes meaningful. The proof is provided in Appendix A.3.

4.6 Planning Regret Under Graph Rollout Error

Rollout error affects planning because actions are selected from predicted graph trajectories. We connect the joint node-edge error recursion to planning regret through a graph-state simulation bound.

Lemma 4 (Planning regret bound).

Assume the reward is Lipschitz with constant LRL_{R} under a graph distance

dG​(G^k,Gk)=c⊤​uk.d_{G}(\hat{G}_{k},G_{k})=c^{\top}u_{k}. (4.18)

Let π^θ\hat{\pi}_{\theta} be the policy selected by planning under the learned GWM, and let π∗\pi^{*} be the policy selected under the true dynamics. Then

J∗​(π∗)−J∗​(π^θ)\displaystyle J^{*}(\pi^{*})-J^{*}(\hat{\pi}_{\theta}) ≤2​LR​‖c‖2​κ​(B)​ϵ~\displaystyle\leq 2L_{R}\|c\|_{2}\kappa(B)\tilde{\epsilon} (4.19)
×ΦH​(γ,ρ​(B))\displaystyle\times\Phi_{H}(\gamma,\rho(B))
+2​ϵR​1−γH1−γ,\displaystyle+2\epsilon_{R}\frac{1-\gamma^{H}}{1-\gamma},

where

ΦH​(γ,ρ)=1ρ−1​[1−(γ​ρ)H1−γ​ρ−1−γH1−γ].\Phi_{H}(\gamma,\rho)=\frac{1}{\rho-1}\left[\frac{1-(\gamma\rho)^{H}}{1-\gamma\rho}-\frac{1-\gamma^{H}}{1-\gamma}\right]. (4.20)

If γ​ρ​(B)>1\gamma\rho(B)>1, the rollout-error contribution grows super-linearly with horizon HH.

Lemma 4 shows that small one-step prediction errors can still cause large planning error when the graph rollout operator is expansive. The factor ρ⁡(B)\rho(B) controls how node and edge errors accumulate, while γ\gamma controls how future errors are weighted in planning. The proof is provided in Appendix A.4.

Corollary 5 (Error level versus error growth slope).

Under the FE recursion in Lemma 1, when the rollout is not dominated by the one-step error floor, the asymptotic log-error growth rate satisfies

∂log⁡ekX∂k→log⁡LX.\frac{\partial\log e^{X}_{k}}{\partial k}\to\log L_{X}. (4.21)

Thus, the slope of the log-error curve can be a more stable indicator of topology-dependent amplification than the final error level.

Corollary 5 explains why level-based metrics can be weak even when topology affects rollout dynamics. In practice, trained models may reach an error floor of order ϵX/(1−LX)\epsilon_{X}/(1-L_{X}), which can mask the relation between GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} and final NodeMSE. Therefore, we report GrowthSlope as an exploratory diagnostic rather than as a pre-registered confirmatory claim. The proof is provided in Appendix A.5.

5 Dataset and Evaluation Protocol

5.1 Graph Topology Generation

We generate seven canonical graph families with distinct spectral and structural properties at N=50N=50 nodes, using three outer seeds for each topology. The topology statistics are summarized in Table 1.

The seven topology families span a broad spectral range, from ρ⁡(A)=2.0\rho(A)=2.0 for chain graphs to ρ⁡(A)=49\rho(A)=49 for complete graphs. They cover three structural regimes: low-connectivity or tree-like graphs (chain, tree), lattice or clustered graphs (grid, small-world), and hub-dominated graphs (scale-free, star, complete). Scale-free graphs are generated by preferential attachment with m=2m=2 edges per new node Barabási and Albert (1999). Small-world graphs use the Watts–Strogatz model with k=4k=4 and rewiring probability p=0.3p=0.3 Watts and Strogatz (1998). All other topologies are deterministic for fixed NN. Each instance stores AA, initial node features X0∈ℝN×8X_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 8}, and the rollout trajectory {Xt,At}t=1T\{X_{t},A_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}.

5.2 Simulators

Fixed-Edge (FE) simulator.

In the FE simulator, the adjacency matrix AA is fixed throughout rollout, matching Section 4.3. Node features evolve according to

Xt=ftrue​(Xt−1,A)+εt,εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I).X_{t}=f_{\rm true}(X_{t-1},A)+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I). (5.1)

Here σ=0.01\sigma=0.01. Node features X∈ℝN×8X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 8} encode state variables such as congestion or utilization. Rollout follows Equation (3.3). The rollout horizon is T=50T=50, and models are evaluated at H∈{1,2,4,8,16,32}H\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\}.

Dynamic-Edge (DE) simulator.

In the DE simulator, both node features and edges evolve during rollout, matching Section 4.4. The edge head follows the dynamic-edge prediction form in Section 3.3:

A^t=σ⁡(Ht​Q​Ht⊤).\hat{A}_{t}=\sigma(H_{t}QH_{t}^{\top}). (5.2)

We use ‖Q‖2=1.0\|Q\|_{2}=1.0 by default. The joint node-edge error follows the operator recursion in Equation (4.14), with the spectral radius given by Equation (4.15). Empirically, this coupling is activated in the DE regime: ρ⁡(B)=132\rho(B)=132–368368, compared with FE values in the range 22–5050. The rollout horizon is T=32T=32.

Agent calling-tree testbed.

The agent calling-tree testbed evaluates GWM rollouts on a heterogeneous task-execution graph. Each instance is a directed acyclic graph with N≈22N\approx 22–3030 nodes, 9 node types, and 6 edge types. Node types include planner, validator, executor, checker, aggregator, reporter, logger, error_handler, and final_answer. Edge types include calls, validates, reports, errors, triggers, and logs. Each node has an 8-dimensional execution-status vector. The primary metric is sink-node success rate, srsink\mathrm{sr}_{\rm sink}, which measures whether the final-answer node reaches a successful terminal state. As calibration, a random policy gives srsink=0.262\mathrm{sr}_{\rm sink}=0.262, while an oracle policy exceeds 0.400.40.

Platform skill-graph testbed.

The platform skill-graph testbed evaluates GWM rollouts on a heterogeneous skill-management graph. Each instance contains N=40N=40 nodes across 8 node types: skill, validator, adapter, artifact, failure_case, patch, task, and tool. The graph models dependencies among skills, validators, adapters, artifacts, and failure-recovery components. The primary metric is skill success rate, srskill\mathrm{sr}_{\rm skill}. Under a no-op policy, srskill\mathrm{sr}_{\rm skill} decays from 1.01.0 to about 0.3170.317 at T=10T=10, showing that skill quality degrades without maintenance actions. R-GCN calibration against the ground-truth simulator gives Pearson r=0.231r=0.231 and MAE =0.029=0.029.

6 Error-Aware GWM

Graph world model setup.

We study GWMs that predict graph-structured states using the transition model in Equation (3.2) and the rollout procedure in Equation (3.3). In the fixed-edge setting, the node-state update follows the GCN-style transition:

X^k+1\displaystyle\hat{X}_{k+1} =tanh⁡(A~​X^k​W1+U​ak)​W2+ξk,\displaystyle=\tanh(\tilde{A}\hat{X}_{k}W_{1}+Ua_{k})W_{2}+\xi_{k}, (6.1)
A~\displaystyle\tilde{A} =D−1/2AD−1/2,\displaystyle=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2},

where A~\tilde{A} is the normalized adjacency matrix and ξk\xi_{k} is i.i.d. rollout noise. This update follows the ActionNode-style GWM formulation of Feng et al. Feng et al. (2025), where actions are injected into the graph state during prediction.

Error-aware training objective.

Our Error-Aware GWM augments the standard prediction objective with three stability terms:

ℒEA=ℒpred+λspec​Rspec+λroll​Rroll+λcrit​Rcrit.\mathcal{L}_{\rm EA}=\mathcal{L}_{\rm pred}+\lambda_{\rm spec}R_{\rm spec}+\lambda_{\rm roll}R_{\rm roll}+\lambda_{\rm crit}R_{\rm crit}. (6.2)

The first term, ℒpred\mathcal{L}_{\rm pred}, is the supervised one-step prediction loss for node states and, in the dynamic-edge setting, edge states. The remaining terms reduce long-horizon rollout instability.

Spectral regularization.

The spectral regularizer controls the model-dependent part of graph error amplification. Motivated by the FE bound in Lemma 1, we penalize large transition-layer spectral norms:

Rspec=∑ℓ‖Wℓ‖22.R_{\rm spec}=\sum_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}^{2}. (6.3)

This term discourages large values of ∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}, reducing the model factor in GEAF^​(G)=ρ⁡(A)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)=\rho(A)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}. It is especially important on high-ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) graphs, where topology already amplifies rollout errors.

Rollout consistency regularization.

The rollout consistency term directly penalizes multi-step prediction drift. Given a rollout horizon set ℋ\mathcal{H}, we define

Rroll=∑h∈ℋ‖X^t+h(h)−Xt+h‖F2,R_{\rm roll}=\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\|\hat{X}_{t+h}^{(h)}-X_{t+h}\|_{F}^{2}, (6.4)

where X^t+h(h)\hat{X}_{t+h}^{(h)} is the hh-step autoregressive prediction produced by repeatedly applying the learned transition model. Unlike one-step training, this term exposes the model to its own rollout distribution and reduces compounding error over long horizons.

Critical-node weighting.

The critical-node term gives larger weight to errors on structurally important nodes. Let wvw_{v} be a normalized centrality-based weight for node vv, such as degree, PageRank, or betweenness centrality. We define

Rcrit=∑v∈Vwv​‖X^t+1,v−Xt+1,v‖22.R_{\rm crit}=\sum_{v\in V}w_{v}\|\hat{X}_{t+1,v}-X_{t+1,v}\|_{2}^{2}. (6.5)

This term reflects that errors on hubs or high-centrality nodes can propagate to many downstream nodes during message passing. By emphasizing critical nodes, Error-Aware GWM reduces the risk that local errors trigger global rollout instability.

Dynamic-edge extension.

For dynamic-edge models, we add the bilinear edge-prediction head from Equation (5.2). The edge loss is binary cross-entropy with weight λe=1.0\lambda_{e}=1.0, and the graph regularization term is

Lg=12​‖W‖2​‖Q‖2.L_{g}=\frac{1}{2}\|W\|_{2}\|Q\|_{2}. (6.6)

This term controls the interaction between node-transition weights WW and edge-prediction weights QQ, which is important because DE rollouts activate the coupled node-edge operator in Equation (4.14).

7 Experiments

7.1 Experimental Setup

Baselines.

We compare six world-model baselines. B1 is an MLP world model (MLP-WM) that does not use graph structure. B2 is a vanilla GCN world model based on graph convolution Kipf and Welling (2017). B3 is an MPNN world model based on neural message passing Gilmer et al. (2017). B4 is a GPS-style graph transformer Rampášek et al. (2022). B5 is an ActionNode GWM based on the fixed-edge architecture of Feng et al. Feng et al. (2025). B6 is our Error-Aware GWM.

Topologies.

We evaluate all baselines on seven synthetic graph families: chain, tree, grid, small-world, scale-free, star, and complete graphs. Each graph has N=50N=50 nodes. Scale-free graphs follow the preferential-attachment model Barabási and Albert (1999), and small-world graphs follow the Watts–Strogatz model Watts and Strogatz (1998). These topologies span a broad spectral range, from ρ⁡(A)=2.0\rho(A)=2.0 for chain graphs to ρ⁡(A)=49.0\rho(A)=49.0 for complete graphs, as summarized in Table 1.

Fixed-edge training.

In the fixed-edge setting, the graph topology is fixed during rollout and each model predicts node states only. We train all six baselines on the FE simulator described in Section 5.2. Evaluation uses rollout horizons H∈{1,2,4,8,16,32}H\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\}, allowing us to measure both short-horizon prediction quality and long-horizon error accumulation, following the standard concern of compounding error in model-based rollout Asadi et al. (2018); Janner et al. (2019).

Dynamic-edge training.

In the dynamic-edge setting, each baseline is extended with the bilinear edge-prediction head in Equation (5.2). The model predicts both node features and edges, and is trained with the node loss, edge BCE loss, and the graph regularizer in Equation (6.6). This setting is related to dynamic graph representation learning You et al. (2022) but differs in that the graph is used as an autoregressive world-model state for rollout prediction. All six baselines are retrained in Stream A across six topologies and three seeds, yielding 6×6×3=1086\times 6\times 3=108 runs.

Heterogeneous agent testbeds.

For the agent calling-tree and platform skill-graph testbeds, we evaluate six R-GCN variants: small, medium, deep, wide, action-node, and critical-node variants. These models handle typed nodes and typed edges in heterogeneous graphs, following the general message-passing view of graph networks Battaglia et al. (2018). Each model is trained for 50 epochs with T-batched forward passes.

7.2 RQ1: Does Topology Predict Rollout-Error Growth?

We first ask whether topology explains the rate at which rollout error grows. The theory predicts that ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) and GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} should appear most clearly in temporal growth, not necessarily in the final error level after optimization and error floors intervene. We therefore test whether higher-GEAF graphs have faster GrowthSlope, and whether this behavior differs from standard GNN over-smoothing.

7.2.1 GEAF tracks error-growth slope

Figure 4 relates log⁡GEAF^\log\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} to GrowthSlope4→32, the slope of the log-NodeMSE curve from horizon 44 to horizon 3232. The trend is positive: runs with larger log⁡GEAF^\log\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} tend to accumulate error faster. This matches Corollary 5, which predicts that topology-dependent amplification should be more visible in the log-error slope than in a single terminal NodeMSE value. The takeaway is not that GEAF alone determines absolute error, but that it tracks the temporal failure mode: high-GEAF graphs are more prone to long-horizon error growth.

7.2.2 Rollout amplification is distinct from over-smoothing

We next compare GWM rollout amplification with classical GNN over-smoothing. The two effects use different operators. Over-smoothing is governed by repeated normalized propagation, which pushes node representations toward a low-variation domain. GWM rollout error is governed by the autoregressive amplification factor GEAF^​(ℓ)=ρ​(A)ℓ​cℓ\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(\ell)=\rho(A)^{\ell}c^{\ell}, where depth and topology jointly affect error growth.

Figure 5 shows this distinction. The over-smoothing operator remains near the normalized propagation domain, while GEAF^​(ℓ)\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(\ell) grows rapidly with message-passing depth and graph spectral radius. Thus, GWM error amplification is not a restatement of standard over-smoothing; it describes a separate rollout-error mechanism.

7.2.3 Global spectral amplification differs from local hub failure

We further separate global spectral amplification from local hub-mediated failure. Figure 6 shows that complete graphs have the largest GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}, consistent with a ρ⁡(A)\rho(A)-dominated global error ceiling. However, star graphs show the largest affected-node fraction under hub injection, despite having lower GEAF than complete graphs. This indicates that global rollout amplification and local failure spread are related but distinct mechanisms: ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) controls the global ceiling, while hub concentration controls localized propagation.

7.2.4 Topology effects strengthen with rollout horizon and edge density

We study how rollout error changes with horizon. The experiment evaluates H∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,48}H\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,48\} across six baselines, seven topologies, and three seeds. Figure 7 reports NodeMSE@HH as a function of rollout horizon.

Low-risk topologies such as chain and tree remain stable over long horizons. High-risk topologies such as scale-free, star, and grid show sharp error growth at larger horizons. This complements the regret analysis: long-horizon behavior is strongly topology-dependent, and short-horizon performance does not fully characterize rollout stability.

We next vary edge density using Erdős–Rényi graphs with edge probability p∈{0.02,0.05,0.10,0.20}p\in\{0.02,0.05,0.10,0.20\}. The experiment compares the vanilla GCN world model, ActionNode GWM, and Error-Aware GWM over three seeds. Figure 8 reports the resulting spectral radius and NodeMSE@32.

As edge density increases, ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) increases. The vanilla GCN world model shows rapidly increasing NodeMSE at high densities, while ActionNode GWM and Error-Aware GWM remain near the low-error floor. This supports the interpretation that edge density affects rollout difficulty through the topology-dependent amplification factor.

7.3 RQ2: Does Rollout Error Affect Planning Regret?

We next test whether prediction error affects downstream planning. GWMs select actions through imagined graph rollouts, so small rollout errors become harmful when they change predicted returns. We measure whether planning regret grows with horizon and whether high-GEAF settings lead to faster regret accumulation.

Figure 9 connects rollout error to downstream planning. Runs with larger GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} tend to have larger regret GrowthSlope from horizon 44 to horizon 3232, consistent with Lemma 4: when the effective graph error operator is larger, imagined trajectories lose reliability faster. The horizon-ratio analysis tells the same story from another angle. Planning regret at horizon 3232 is substantially larger than one-step regret across every topology, showing that the planning failure is a long-horizon rollout effect rather than a one-step artifact.

7.4 RQ3: Does Error-Aware GWM Improve Long-Horizon Stability?

We evaluate whether Error-Aware GWM stabilizes long-horizon rollout without sacrificing accuracy. This RQ compares the full objective with vanilla GCN rollouts and simpler stabilizers such as gradient clipping, weight decay, and spectral-norm projection. We also test robustness under graph rewiring, noisy observations, and graph-size scaling.

7.4.1 Error-Aware GWM prevents divergence while preserving accuracy

Figure 10 gives the central FE comparison. On high-risk scale-free and star topologies, the vanilla GCN world model enters an exploding-error regime as the horizon grows, while Error-Aware GWM stays near the low-error floor. Across all paired topology-seed cells, the full objective eliminates the divergences observed in the vanilla GCN setting. The result supports the design principle behind Error-Aware GWM: spectral control is most useful when paired with rollout consistency and critical-node weighting, so the model remains both stable and predictive.

7.4.2 Ablation: Stability alone is not enough

Table 2 shows that simple stabilizers reduce divergence, but they neither eliminate it nor preserve prediction accuracy. Weight decay and spectral-norm projection lower divergence to 4/21 cells, yet their median NodeMSE@32 remains orders of magnitude larger than Error-Aware GWM. Spectral-norm projection is 1690×1690\times worse than Error-Aware GWM, while weight decay collapses toward a near-constant predictor. The advantage of Error-Aware GWM is therefore not only divergence reduction; it is the combination of stability and predictive accuracy.

7.4.3 Robustness to topology perturbation, noise, and graph size.

Graph Rewiring Robustness.

We evaluate how topology rewiring affects long-horizon rollout error on the scale-free topology. We compare six rewiring operations: identity, PageRank-based edge removal, random edge addition, random edge flipping, sparsification, and densification. The evaluation covers the vanilla GCN world model, ActionNode GWM, and Error-Aware GWM over three seeds.

Figure 11 shows that the vanilla GCN world model remains in a high-error regime across all rewiring methods. ActionNode GWM is stable under most rewiring operations but shows higher error under densification and random edge addition. Error-Aware GWM remains stable across all rewiring types, with NodeMSE@H=20H=20 in the range of approximately 2.02.0–5.0×10−45.0\times 10^{-4}. This supports the role of spectral regularization in controlling topology-induced rollout error under graph perturbations.

Robustness to Noisy Graph Observations.

We test whether observation noise is the main source of rollout instability. Gaussian noise with σ∈{0,10−3,10−2,0.05,0.1,0.2}\sigma\in\{0,10^{-3},10^{-2},0.05,0.1,0.2\} is added to graph observations before rollout evaluation. Figure 12 reports NodeMSE@H=20H=20 across baselines.

Most baselines remain nearly unchanged as observation noise increases, while the vanilla GCN world model is already in a high-error regime at σ=0\sigma=0. Thus, the observed rollout instability is mainly driven by model-topology dynamics rather than small Gaussian observation noise.

Graph Size Scaling.

We evaluate graph-size scaling over N∈{20,50,100,200,500}N\in\{20,50,100,200,500\} across five topologies, six baselines, and three seeds. Figure 13 reports GEAF^\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}} and NodeMSE@32 as functions of graph size.

Across graph sizes, ActionNode GWM, GPS, and Error-Aware GWM remain near the low-error regime, while the vanilla GCN world model exhibits large rollout errors on high-risk cells. MPNN runs encounter out-of-memory failures at larger graph sizes due to dense message tensors. These results show that the stability patterns observed at N=50N=50 persist across a broader graph-size range.

7.5 RQ4: When Does Dynamic-Edge Coupling Matter?

We study when node-edge coupling matters. In FE models, edges are fixed and the coupling term is dormant. In DE models, edge prediction allows node and edge errors to affect each other. We test whether DE training improves DE rollout accuracy and whether the spectral witness ρ⁡(B)>max⁡(LX,MA)\rho(B)>\max(L_{X},M_{A}) appears in trained models.

7.5.1 DE training improves DE rollout accuracy

We evaluate whether training on dynamic-edge trajectories improves rollout accuracy in DE environments. The paired comparison uses n=36n=36 paired cells: ActionNode GWM and Error-Aware GWM across six topologies and three seeds. Each pair compares a model trained only on fixed-edge trajectories but evaluated on DE rollouts against the same architecture trained directly on DE trajectories.

Dynamic-edge training substantially improves DE rollout accuracy. The improvement holds for both ActionNode GWM and Error-Aware GWM, and every paired comparison favors DE training. This supports Lemma 2: in DE environments, the model must learn node dynamics and the edge-prediction pathway through which node and edge errors interact. FE-trained models lack this pathway and are systematically mismatched to evolving graph structure.

7.5.2 DE models activate node-edge coupling

We test whether the joint node-edge operator in Lemma 2 becomes active when the model is trained with an edge-prediction head. In the DE regime, the edge predictor creates a node-to-edge pathway with MX>0M_{X}>0, while message passing provides an edge-to-node pathway with LA>0L_{A}>0. Therefore, the lemma predicts the spectral witness

ρ⁡(B)>max⁡(LX,MA)\rho(B)>\max(L_{X},M_{A}) (7.1)

whenever the coupling is non-degenerate.

Across all 108 DE-trained cells, the witness holds in 108/108 cases, with sign-test p<10−30p<10^{-30} and mean excess approximately 155155 (Table 3). Since the inequality follows mathematically once LA​MX>0L_{A}M_{X}>0, the empirical content is the magnitude rather than only the direction. The large excess shows that learned DE models do not collapse to a nearly fixed-edge solution; they learn substantive node-edge coupling.

7.5.3 FE models show dormant coupling and perturbation contraction

In the FE regime, the edge-prediction head is absent, so MX=0M_{X}=0 and the joint operator reduces to node-only dynamics. The super-additive witness in Equation (7.1) therefore cannot activate. Figure 14 supports this distinction. The left panel shows injected perturbations decaying rapidly to the numerical floor, indicating contractive FE dynamics. The right panel shows that Error-Aware GWM substantially lowers GEAF compared with ActionNode GWM, consistent with spectral regularization reducing the rollout amplification ceiling.

Figure 15 decomposes FE-regime GrowthSlope under node-only, edge-only, and joint perturbation injection. Node-only perturbations have consistently negative slopes, indicating self-correction under contractive FE dynamics. Edge-only slopes are close to zero, and joint slopes closely follow edge-only slopes. This is consistent with the FE structure MX=0M_{X}=0, where the joint node-edge operator does not activate cross-coupling.

7.5.4 OOD perturbation confirms the FE contraction boundary

We perform an OOD amplitude retest by training on chain graphs and evaluating on scale-free graphs. Perturbation amplitudes are swept over δ∈{0.1,0.5,1.0,2.0}\delta\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0,2.0\}, and injections are applied to six positions. Figure 16 reports NodeMSE@H=20H=20 for the vanilla GCN world model, which is the only baseline with a measurable nonzero signal in this setting.

NodeMSE increases with perturbation amplitude across all injection positions. However, the pre-registered high-risk position tests do not reject after Holm correction. For the other baselines, perturbations remain absorbed with NodeMSE below the measurement floor. These results support the scope interpretation that FE dynamics are strongly contractive for most architectures, while measurable OOD sensitivity appears mainly in the vanilla GCN world model.

7.5.5 Regime interpretation

Candidate mechanisms.

The regime-conditional behavior of the joint operator can be explained by four mechanisms. First, in the FE regime, the edge-prediction head is absent, so MX=0M_{X}=0 by construction and the coupling product LA​MXL_{A}M_{X} is structurally zero. Second, Error-Aware GWM reduces the effective node-transition gain by spectral regularization, making FE perturbations more likely to contract. Third, if the coupling product is positive but small, longer horizons may be required for the asymptotic rate to appear; this explanation does not apply when MX=0M_{X}=0. Fourth, small perturbations may remain in a local linear regime whose Jacobian is much smaller than the global Lipschitz bound. The multi-axis sweep over perturbation size and horizon separates these cases and supports the FE contraction interpretation.

Regime interpretation.

These results support a regime-conditional view of graph rollout error. Fixed-edge GWM corresponds to the MX=0M_{X}=0 corner of the joint-operator framework, where node-edge cross-coupling is dormant. Dynamic-edge training activates the off-diagonal coupling terms and changes the effective rollout-error operator. The framework therefore does not replace fixed-edge GWM; it explains when fixed-edge dynamics are sufficient and when dynamic-edge training is required.

7.6 RQ5: How Do GWMs Behave on Heterogeneous Agent Graphs?

We evaluate GWMs on heterogeneous agent and skill graphs, where nodes have roles such as planner, executor, validator, tool, and failure handler. This RQ tests whether rollout failures depend on role structure, whether R-GCN rollouts are calibrated against simulators, and whether correction policies can reduce agent-level errors.

7.6.1 Calibration against heterogeneous simulators

We calibrate the R-GCN rollout models against the ground-truth heterogeneous simulators on the agent calling-tree and platform skill-graph testbeds. Figure 17 compares R-GCN predictions with simulator outputs after the sigmoid-head fix. On the agent calling-tree testbed, the R-GCN mean is 0.4420.442 versus ground-truth mean 0.4370.437, with Pearson r=0.311r=0.311 and MAE =0.051=0.051. On the skill-graph testbed, the R-GCN mean is 0.3870.387 versus ground-truth mean 0.4060.406, with Pearson r=0.231r=0.231 and MAE =0.029=0.029.

These results show that the R-GCN models are reasonably calibrated in mean and absolute error, but their instance-level correlations are weak to moderate. We therefore use the heterogeneous R-GCN results as agent-graph stress tests and calibration evidence, not as a high-precision replacement for the ground-truth simulator.

7.6.2 Role-dependent failure sensitivity

We evaluate whether different functional subgraphs contribute differently to agent-task success. We mask role-specific subgraphs in the agent calling-tree testbed and measure both success-rate drop and trajectory-level NodeMSE. Figure 18 shows that full-graph masking gives the largest degradation, as expected. Among partial masks, hub and validator-related components produce larger changes than leaf masking, while leaf masking has almost no effect.

These results support role-dependent error amplification. Not all nodes contribute equally to rollout quality: masking structurally or functionally central components has a larger effect than masking peripheral leaves.

We evaluate how injected errors propagate across different functional roles in the agent calling-tree testbed. We inject perturbations into planner, validator, hub, bridge, and random nodes across 20 instances. Figure 19 reports failure propagation depth (FPD) and the number of error nodes at the final timestep.

Planner and validator injections produce median FPD around 3, while bridge and hub injections have smaller median FPD. Random injection has the largest median FPD at 4. The final error-node counts are broadly similar across injection types, but the distributions vary by role. These results show that failure propagation depends on functional role, not only graph position.

7.6.3 Correction policies

We also test whether a local GEAF proxy can guide node-level correction policies in heterogeneous agent graphs. In the current FE formulation,

GEAF^local​(v)=degree⁡(v)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2.\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}_{\rm local}(v)=\mathrm{degree}(v)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}. (7.2)

Since ∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2} is global for a fixed model, GEAF^local​(v)\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}_{\rm local}(v) induces the same node ranking as degree centrality. Figure 20 confirms this equivalence: the GEAF-proxy policy and the degree policy achieve the same mean error reduction of 12.9%, outperforming random correction but remaining below the oracle policy at 22.4%. Thus, local GEAF is useful as a non-random structural heuristic, but in this FE setting it does not provide a distinct correction signal beyond degree centrality.

We next compare node correction policies under a 10% correction budget. Figure 21 reports NodeMSE reduction across six baselines, six topologies, and three seeds. Oracle correction gives the strongest upper-bound performance. Among practical policies, uncertainty-based correction gives the largest average gain over random correction. GEAF-proxy correction improves over random but is indistinguishable from degree-based correction.

This result is consistent with the FE local-GEAF identity. When model weights are fixed, the local GEAF score reduces to a degree-proportional ranking:

GEAF^local​(v)=degree⁡(v)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2.\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}_{\rm local}(v)=\mathrm{degree}(v)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}. (7.3)

Thus, GEAF is useful as a non-random structural heuristic, but in this FE correction setting it does not provide a distinct node-ranking signal beyond degree centrality.

We also compare correction policies on the agent calling-tree testbed under a 10% node-correction budget. The policies include random, degree, GEAF-proxy, and oracle correction. Figure 22 reports the reduction in error-flag mean.

The oracle policy gives the largest reduction, while GEAF-proxy and degree correction are tied because they induce the same node ranking in this FE local formulation. This supports the scope statement that local GEAF is a useful structural heuristic but does not provide a distinct correction signal beyond degree centrality in the FE agent-graph setting.

7.6.4 Long-horizon agent task completion

We evaluate agent task completion on the agent calling-tree and platform skill-graph testbeds. We pool 160 instances per testbed and report task success rate (SR) at horizons H∈{1,5,10,20}H\in\{1,5,10,20\}. Results are averaged over 6 testbed-seed cells for each baseline and horizon.

Table 4 and Figure 23 show that architecture choice has limited impact on heterogeneous agent-task completion. At H=1H=1, all methods cluster around SR≈0.49\approx 0.49. For H≥5H\geq 5, all methods decline toward SR≈0.42\approx 0.42. Thus, the long-horizon planning challenge persists even with graph-structured world models.

These real-world evaluations clarify the boundary of GWMs. Specialized graph classifiers remain stronger on static node classification, GWM variants are competitive but not dominant on temporal link prediction, and all methods struggle on long-horizon heterogeneous agent planning. GWMs are therefore best viewed as a framework for dynamic graph rollouts and agent planning, not as a replacement for task-specific graph learning methods. Error-Aware regularization provides modest real-world gains, with its strongest benefit in controlled rollout regimes where long-horizon error accumulation is the main failure mode.

7.7 RQ6: What Is the Real-World Scope of GWMs?

Finally, we test GWMs on standard real-world graph benchmarks to clarify their practical boundary. These experiments compare GWM variants with specialized graph baselines on static node classification and temporal link prediction. The goal is not to claim state-of-the-art performance, but to identify where GWMs remain competitive and where task-specific graph models are preferable.

7.7.1 Static Node Classification on Cora and Citeseer

We first evaluate static node classification on Cora and Citeseer Yang et al. (2016). Cora contains 2,708 nodes, 5,278 edges, and 7 classes; Citeseer contains 3,327 nodes, 4,732 edges, and 6 classes. We follow the standard public train/validation/test split. The baselines are GCN Kipf and Welling (2017), GAT Veličković et al. (2018), and GraphSAGE Hamilton et al. (2017). All models are trained for 200 epochs with Adam, learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, dropout 0.50.5, and 3 random seeds.

Table 5 and Figure 24 show that specialized static graph classifiers remain stronger on Cora. GCN achieves the best Cora accuracy at 80.6%, while FE-GWM and Error-Aware GWM achieve 73.5% and 75.0%, respectively. On Citeseer, the gap is smaller: all methods fall within an approximately 3 pp range, with GAT best at 68.1% and Error-Aware GWM reaching 66.9%. Error-Aware GWM consistently improves over FE-GWM by 1–1.5 pp, suggesting that spectral regularization is mildly beneficial even in a static regime.

7.7.2 Temporal Link Prediction on Bitcoin-Alpha

We evaluate temporal link prediction on Bitcoin-Alpha (Kumar et al., 2019), a sparse temporal trust network with 3,783 nodes and 24,186 temporal edges. We construct 60-day windows and compare GWM variants with a JODIE-style temporal interaction model (Kumar et al., 2019) and a static GCN baseline. We report AP, AUC, and MRR over 3 seeds.

Table 6 and Figure 25 show that GWM variants are competitive but do not dominate specialized baselines. FE-GWM achieves the best AP, while Static GCN has the best AUC and JODIE-style has the best MRR. DE-GWM and Error-Aware DE-GWM do not consistently improve over FE-GWM, suggesting that dynamic-edge modeling is most useful when edge dynamics provide stable predictive signal over the rollout horizon.

8 Additional Experiments

This section provides concise result summaries for all other experiments.

8.1 Seed Stability of Error Metrics

We first check whether the observed error patterns are artifacts of random seed choice. Figure 26 reports seed-level distributions of NodeMSE@32 and GrowthSlope across the seven topology families. The distributions are stable across seeds, and deterministic topologies show limited variation. This supports the use of three outer seeds in the main experiments and suggests that the observed GEAF-related trends are not driven by a small number of random graph instances.

8.2 Multi-Hop Error Propagation Is Limited Under Contractive FE Dynamics

We test whether local perturbations propagate across multiple graph hops. We inject perturbations at depths {1,2,4,6,8,10}\{1,2,4,6,8,10\} on chain and scale-free graphs across six baselines and three seeds. Figure 27 shows that multi-hop error propagation is limited for all non-diverged models. On chain graphs, NodeMSE@H=20H=20 remains below 10−1210^{-12} across all injection depths, with failure propagation depth close to 1. On scale-free graphs, all non-diverged models remain below 10−1310^{-13}, while the diverged GCN baseline reaches NodeMSE@H=20H=20 around 101010^{10}.

This result supports a regime-specific interpretation: FE dynamics are often contractive and absorb local perturbations, while severe multi-hop amplification appears mainly when the underlying baseline has already entered a divergent rollout regime.

8.3 Zero-Shot Topology Shift

We test zero-shot generalization under topology shift by training on one topology and evaluating on another. The evaluated train–test pairs are chain→\togrid, grid→\tosmall-world, small-world→\toscale-free, scale-free→\tostar, and tree→\toscale-free. The experiment covers six baselines and three seeds.

Figure 28 shows that cross-topology transfer causes a large increase in NodeMSE@H=20H=20. Excluding diverged vanilla GCN cells, the median NodeMSE@H=20H=20 across baselines is 0.1960.196, compared with an in-distribution level of approximately 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. Error-Aware GWM obtains a median of 0.1830.183, which is slightly better than the overall median but still far above the in-distribution floor. These results indicate that zero-shot topology shift is a structural difficulty for graph rollouts, not merely an architecture-specific failure.

8.4 Sparse and Dense Message-Passing Layers

We compare sparse and dense message-passing behavior on the scale-free topology. The experiment evaluates the vanilla GCN world model, MPNN world model, and GPS-style graph transformer across rollout horizons H∈{1,4,8,16,32}H\in\{1,4,8,16,32\} and three seeds.

Figure 29 shows that the vanilla GCN world model diverges as the horizon increases, with median NodeMSE@H=32H=32 reaching 6.5×1096.5\times 10^{9}. In contrast, MPNN and GPS remain near the low-error floor, with median NodeMSE@H=32H=32 equal to 2.2×10−42.2\times 10^{-4} and 4.0×10−44.0\times 10^{-4}, respectively. This suggests that the observed divergence is not explained by message-passing density alone. Instead, it is tied to the interaction between the GCN transition operator and the high-risk scale-free topology.

8.5 Directed and Undirected Graph Variants

We evaluate whether graph directionality affects rollout growth. The experiment uses chain, tree, and scale-free graphs with directed and undirected variants, covering three baselines and three seeds. Figure 30 reports GrowthSlope8→32.

Directionality changes the error-growth distribution, especially on scale-free graphs, where the variance is larger. Chain and tree graphs show smaller directionality effects. These results indicate that directed edges can change the effective rollout operator, but the effect depends strongly on topology.

8.6 Temporal Memory Variants

We compare temporal-memory variants for long-horizon rollout prediction. The main ablation evaluates Markov, last-2, and last-4 history variants on scale-free and small-world graphs. The extended experiment compares recurrent, transformer, and retrieval-augmented memory architectures. Figure 31 reports NodeMSE@HH across rollout horizons.

Last-kk history reduces NodeMSE relative to the Markov variant, with most of the gain appearing from the last-2 context. In the extended comparison, retrieval-augmented memory achieves lower long-horizon NodeMSE than recurrent and transformer variants. These results suggest that adding temporal context can improve long-horizon rollout accuracy, especially when the memory mechanism provides stable retrieval rather than only recurrent propagation.

9 Conclusion

We present a unified framework for analyzing and improving Graph World Models in graph-structured planning environments. The framework covers fixed-edge and dynamic-edge regimes, introduces topology-aware rollout-error analysis through GEAF and the joint node-edge operator BB, and connects rollout error to planning regret. Empirically, long-horizon graph planning is sensitive to topology and regime: regret increases with rollout horizon, dynamic-edge training is needed when graph structure evolves, and Error-Aware GWM improves stability while preserving prediction accuracy. Real-world experiments show that GWMs are best viewed as tools for dynamic graph rollouts and agent planning, not as replacements for specialized graph learning methods. Future work includes applying this framework to LLM-based multi-agent systems, heterogeneous knowledge graphs, and real-time network planning.

10 Discussion

Our results show that GWM rollout error is regime-dependent. In fixed-edge settings, instability mainly comes from the interaction between topology and the learned node-transition operator. This explains why the vanilla GCN world model fails on high-ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) graphs, while Error-Aware GWM avoids divergence by combining spectral control, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting. In dynamic-edge settings, edge prediction activates node-edge cross-coupling through the joint operator BB, and DE training substantially improves DE rollout accuracy. GEAF is therefore best interpreted as a topology-aware indicator of rollout-error growth, not as a universal predictor of final error level. Locally, the FE version of GEAF reduces to degree centrality, so future correction policies should use activation-dependent, uncertainty-aware, or DE-regime coupling terms to provide a distinct node-priority signal.

11 Limitations and Future Work

The strongest evidence in this work comes from controlled synthetic graph simulators. Real-world benchmarks show more limited transfer: GWMs are not replacements for specialized static graph classifiers, and DE-GWM does not consistently dominate on sparse temporal link prediction. The joint-operator theory is also only partially tested: FE models collapse to the MX=0M_{X}=0 case, while larger DE datasets are needed to evaluate the GEAF proxy for ρ⁡(B)\rho(B). Future work should study larger and denser temporal graphs, real agent-system traces, activation-aware local GEAF, uncertainty-guided correction, and memory-augmented GWMs for long-horizon planning.

Appendix A Proofs and mathematical background

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

Proof.

Since the graph is fixed in the FE regime, we have At≡AA_{t}\equiv A for all rollout steps. Let FθX​(⋅,A,a)F_{\theta}^{X}(\cdot,A,a) denote the learned node-transition map and FX⋆(⋅,A,a)F^{X\star}(\cdot,A,a) denote the true node-transition map. By Assumption 2, for any input (X,A,a)(X,A,a) in the compact state space,

∥FθX(X,A,a)−FX⋆(X,A,a)∥F≤ϵX.\|F_{\theta}^{X}(X,A,a)-F^{X\star}(X,A,a)\|_{F}\leq\epsilon_{X}. (A.1)

Let X^k\hat{X}_{k} and XkX_{k} be the predicted and true node features at rollout step kk. Then

ek+1X\displaystyle e^{X}_{k+1} =‖X^k+1−Xk+1‖F\displaystyle=\|\hat{X}_{k+1}-X_{k+1}\|_{F} (A.2)
=∥FθX(X^k,A,ak)−FX⋆(Xk,A,ak)∥F.\displaystyle=\|F_{\theta}^{X}(\hat{X}_{k},A,a_{k})-F^{X\star}(X_{k},A,a_{k})\|_{F}.

Adding and subtracting FθX​(Xk,A,ak)F_{\theta}^{X}(X_{k},A,a_{k}) and applying the triangle inequality gives

ek+1X\displaystyle e^{X}_{k+1} ≤‖FθX​(X^k,A,ak)−FθX​(Xk,A,ak)‖F\displaystyle\leq\|F_{\theta}^{X}(\hat{X}_{k},A,a_{k})-F_{\theta}^{X}(X_{k},A,a_{k})\|_{F} (A.3)
+∥FθX(Xk,A,ak)−FX⋆(Xk,A,ak)∥F.\displaystyle+\|F_{\theta}^{X}(X_{k},A,a_{k})-F^{X\star}(X_{k},A,a_{k})\|_{F}.

The second term is bounded by ϵX\epsilon_{X} from Equation (A.1). For the first term, Assumption 3 gives a message-passing node transition with coordinate-wise Lipschitz activation σ\sigma:

FθX​(X,A,a)=σ⁡(A^​X​W1+U​a​𝟏⊤)​W2.F_{\theta}^{X}(X,A,a)=\sigma(\hat{A}XW_{1}+Ua\mathbf{1}^{\top})W_{2}. (A.4)

For a multi-layer message-passing model, repeated use of the Lipschitz property of σ\sigma and submultiplicativity of operator norms gives

‖FθX​(X^k,A,ak)−FθX​(Xk,A,ak)‖F\displaystyle\|F_{\theta}^{X}(\hat{X}_{k},A,a_{k})-F_{\theta}^{X}(X_{k},A,a_{k})\|_{F} (A.5)
≤Lσ​‖A‖2​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2⋅‖X^k−Xk‖F.\displaystyle\leq L_{\sigma}\|A\|_{2}\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}\cdot\|\hat{X}_{k}-X_{k}\|_{F}.

For symmetric adjacency matrices, ‖A‖2=ρ⁡(A)\|A\|_{2}=\rho(A). Hence,

‖FθX​(X^k,A,ak)−FθX​(Xk,A,ak)‖F≤LX​ekX,\displaystyle\|F_{\theta}^{X}(\hat{X}_{k},A,a_{k})-F_{\theta}^{X}(X_{k},A,a_{k})\|_{F}\leq L_{X}e^{X}_{k}, (A.6)
LX=Lσ​ρ​(A)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2.\displaystyle L_{X}=L_{\sigma}\rho(A)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}.

Combining Equations (A.3) and (A.6), we obtain the affine recursion

ek+1X≤LX​ekX+ϵX.e^{X}_{k+1}\leq L_{X}e^{X}_{k}+\epsilon_{X}. (A.7)

Unrolling Equation (A.7) for kk steps yields

ekX≤LXk​e0X+ϵX​∑i=0k−1LXi.e^{X}_{k}\leq L_{X}^{k}e^{X}_{0}+\epsilon_{X}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{X}^{i}. (A.8)

If LX≠1L_{X}\neq 1, the finite geometric sum gives

∑i=0k−1LXi=LXk−1LX−1.\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{X}^{i}=\frac{L_{X}^{k}-1}{L_{X}-1}. (A.9)

Therefore,

ekX≤LXk​e0X+ϵX​LXk−1LX−1.e^{X}_{k}\leq L_{X}^{k}e^{X}_{0}+\epsilon_{X}\frac{L_{X}^{k}-1}{L_{X}-1}. (A.10)

This proves Lemma 1. When LX=1L_{X}=1, the same recursion gives the limiting form ekX≤e0X+k​ϵXe^{X}_{k}\leq e^{X}_{0}+k\epsilon_{X}. ∎

A.2 Proof of Lemma 2

Proof.

By assumption, the node and edge rollout errors satisfy

ek+1X\displaystyle e^{X}_{k+1} ≤LX​ekX+LA​ekA+ϵX,\displaystyle\leq L_{X}e^{X}_{k}+L_{A}e^{A}_{k}+\epsilon_{X}, (A.11)
ek+1A\displaystyle e^{A}_{k+1} ≤MX​ekX+MA​ekA+ϵA.\displaystyle\leq M_{X}e^{X}_{k}+M_{A}e^{A}_{k}+\epsilon_{A}.

B\displaystyle B =(LXLAMXMA),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}L_{X}&L_{A}\\ M_{X}&M_{A}\end{pmatrix},
ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =(ϵX,ϵA)⊤.\displaystyle=(\epsilon_{X},\epsilon_{A})^{\top}.

Since all constants are nonnegative, Equation (A.11) is equivalent to the componentwise vector inequality

uk+1⪯B​uk+ϵ.u_{k+1}\preceq Bu_{k}+\epsilon. (A.13)

This proves Equation (4.14).

It remains to compute ρ⁡(B)\rho(B). The characteristic polynomial of BB is

det(λ​I−B)\displaystyle\det(\lambda I-B) =λ2−(LX+MA)​λ\displaystyle=\lambda^{2}-(L_{X}+M_{A})\lambda (A.14)
+(LX​MA−LA​MX).\displaystyle+(L_{X}M_{A}-L_{A}M_{X}).

λ±\displaystyle\lambda_{\pm} =12[(LX+MA)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(L_{X}+M_{A}) (A.15)
±(LX−MA)2+4​LA​MX].\displaystyle\pm\sqrt{(L_{X}-M_{A})^{2}+4L_{A}M_{X}}\Big].

Because BB is nonnegative, Perron–Frobenius implies that its spectral radius is the larger eigenvalue. Hence,

ρ⁡(B)\displaystyle\rho(B) =λ+\displaystyle=\lambda_{+} (A.16)
=12[(LX+MA)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(L_{X}+M_{A})
+(LX−MA)2+4​LA​MX].\displaystyle+\sqrt{(L_{X}-M_{A})^{2}+4L_{A}M_{X}}\Big].

This proves Equation (4.15).

Finally, suppose LA​MX>0L_{A}M_{X}>0. Then

(LX−MA)2+4​LA​MX\displaystyle(L_{X}-M_{A})^{2}+4L_{A}M_{X} >(LX−MA)2,\displaystyle>(L_{X}-M_{A})^{2}, (A.17)
(LX−MA)2+4​LA​MX\displaystyle\sqrt{(L_{X}-M_{A})^{2}+4L_{A}M_{X}} >|LX−MA|.\displaystyle>|L_{X}-M_{A}|.

=max⁡(LX,MA).\displaystyle=\max(L_{X},M_{A}).

A.3 Proof of Lemma 3

Proof.

Since BB is a nonnegative matrix, the Gershgorin circle theorem gives

ρ⁡(B)≤max⁡(LX+LA,MX+MA).\rho(B)\leq\max(L_{X}+L_{A},M_{X}+M_{A}). (A.19)

In the signal-dominant regime, the first-row error term is controlled by the topology-dependent message-passing contribution plus a bounded non-topological residual. Thus,

LX+LA\displaystyle L_{X}+L_{A} ≤GEAF^​(G)+GEAF^​(G)​RX‖A‖2\displaystyle\leq\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)+\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)\frac{R_{X}}{\|A\|_{2}} (A.20)
=GEAF^​(G)​(1+RX‖A‖2).\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)\left(1+\frac{R_{X}}{\|A\|_{2}}\right).

Under the same signal-dominant condition, the second row is no larger than this bound, so combining Equations (A.19) and (A.20) yields

ρ⁡(B)≤GEAF^​(G)​(1+RX‖A‖2).\rho(B)\leq\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)\left(1+\frac{R_{X}}{\|A\|_{2}}\right). (A.21)

Since ‖A‖2≥RX\|A\|_{2}\geq R_{X}, we have

1+RX‖A‖2≤2.1+\frac{R_{X}}{\|A\|_{2}}\leq 2. (A.22)

Therefore,

ρ⁡(B)\displaystyle\rho(B) ≤GEAF^​(G)​(1+RX‖A‖2)\displaystyle\leq\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)\left(1+\frac{R_{X}}{\|A\|_{2}}\right) (A.23)
≤2​GEAF^​(G).\displaystyle\leq 2\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G).

This proves the bound in Equation (4.17).

Finally, if model weights are fixed across topologies, then

GEAF^​(G)=ρ⁡(A)​∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2.\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G)=\rho(A)\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2}. (A.24)

The factor ∏ℓ‖Wℓ‖2\prod_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{2} is constant across topologies. Hence, GEAF^​(G)\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G) is monotone in ρ⁡(A)\rho(A), and the rank order of GEAF^​(G)\widehat{\mathrm{GEAF}}(G) matches the rank order of ρ⁡(A)\rho(A). This proves Lemma 3. ∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 4

Proof.

Let π∗\pi^{*} be the policy selected by planning with the true dynamics, and let π^θ\hat{\pi}_{\theta} be the policy selected by planning with the learned GWM. A standard simulation-lemma argument bounds the regret by the accumulated reward error along the planning horizon:

−Rθ(G^k,ak)|.\displaystyle-R_{\theta}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k})\Big|.
