|R⋆​(Gk,ak)−Rθ​(G^k,ak)|\displaystyle\left|R^{\star}(G_{k},a_{k})-R_{\theta}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k})\right| (A.26)
≤|R⋆​(Gk,ak)−R⋆​(G^k,ak)|\displaystyle\leq\left|R^{\star}(G_{k},a_{k})-R^{\star}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k})\right|
+|R⋆​(G^k,ak)−Rθ​(G^k,ak)|.\displaystyle+\left|R^{\star}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k})-R_{\theta}(\hat{G}_{k},a_{k})\right|.

≤LR​dG​(Gk,G^k)+ϵR.\displaystyle\leq L_{R}d_{G}(G_{k},\hat{G}_{k})+\epsilon_{R}.

dG​(Gk,G^k)=c⊤​uk≤‖c‖2​‖uk‖2.d_{G}(G_{k},\hat{G}_{k})=c^{\top}u_{k}\leq\|c\|_{2}\|u_{k}\|_{2}. (A.28)

From Lemma 2, the joint error recursion satisfies

uk+1⪯B​uk+ϵ.u_{k+1}\preceq Bu_{k}+\epsilon. (A.29)

‖uk‖2≤κ⁡(B)​ϵ~​∑i=0k−1ρ​(B)i.\|u_{k}\|_{2}\leq\kappa(B)\tilde{\epsilon}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\rho(B)^{i}. (A.30)

J∗​(π∗)−J∗​(π^θ)\displaystyle J^{*}(\pi^{*})-J^{*}(\hat{\pi}_{\theta}) ≤2​LR​‖c‖2​κ​(B)​ϵ~\displaystyle\leq 2L_{R}\|c\|_{2}\kappa(B)\tilde{\epsilon} (A.31)

+2ϵR∑k=0H−1γk.\displaystyle+2\epsilon_{R}\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}.

The reward-model error term is

∑k=0H−1γk=1−γH1−γ.\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}=\frac{1-\gamma^{H}}{1-\gamma}. (A.32)

For the rollout-error term,

∑k=0H−1γk​∑i=0k−1ρi\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\rho^{i} =∑k=0H−1γk​ρk−1ρ−1\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\frac{\rho^{k}-1}{\rho-1} (A.33)
=1ρ−1​[∑k=0H−1(γ​ρ)k−∑k=0H−1γk]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho-1}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}(\gamma\rho)^{k}-\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\right]
=1ρ−1​[1−(γ​ρ)H1−γ​ρ−1−γH1−γ].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho-1}\left[\frac{1-(\gamma\rho)^{H}}{1-\gamma\rho}-\frac{1-\gamma^{H}}{1-\gamma}\right].

Thus,

A.5 Proof of Corollary 5

Proof.

From Lemma 1, the FE rollout error satisfies

ekX≤LXk​e0X+ϵX​LXk−1LX−1.e^{X}_{k}\leq L_{X}^{k}e^{X}_{0}+\epsilon_{X}\frac{L_{X}^{k}-1}{L_{X}-1}. (A.36)

When the rollout is not dominated by the constant error floor, the leading dependence on kk is proportional to LXkL_{X}^{k}. Thus, for some constant C>0C>0 independent of kk,

ekX≈C​LXk.e^{X}_{k}\approx CL_{X}^{k}. (A.37)

Taking logarithms gives

log⁡ekX≈log⁡C+k​log⁡LX.\log e^{X}_{k}\approx\log C+k\log L_{X}. (A.38)

Therefore,

∂log⁡ekX∂k→log⁡LX.\frac{\partial\log e^{X}_{k}}{\partial k}\to\log L_{X}. (A.39)

This proves Corollary 5. ∎

Appendix B Auxiliary latent world-model bounds

B.1 Latent world-model setup

This appendix records the scalar latent-world-model bounds that underlie the graph-valued results in the main text. They are not a replacement for Lemmas 1–4; rather, they show how the familiar compounding-error argument for latent dynamics Hafner et al. (2018); Chua et al. (2018); Janner et al. (2019) becomes the graph-specific operator analysis used in Section 4. We consider a sequential decision-making setting in which an agent interacts with a partially observed environment over discrete time steps. At each time step tt, the agent receives an observation ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}, selects an action at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}, and receives a scalar reward rt∈ℝr_{t}\in\mathbb{R}. Since the true environment state is generally not directly observable, the agent must infer a compact latent state from its interaction history. Let

ht=(o1,a1,o2,a2,…,ot)h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},o_{2},a_{2},\ldots,o_{t}) (B.1)

denote the observable history up to time tt. A latent world model learns an internal state representation

zt=eθ​(ht),z_{t}=e_{\theta}(h_{t}), (B.2)

where zt∈𝒵z_{t}\in\mathcal{Z} is a latent state and eθe_{\theta} is an encoder parameterized by θ\theta.

The purpose of the latent world model is not only to encode the current observation, but also to predict how the latent state evolves under actions. We define a latent world model as

𝒲θ=(CLOSE\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{\theta}=( eθ,pθ​(zt+1∣zt,at),\displaystyle e_{\theta},\,p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t}), (B.3)
OPENpθ​(ot∣zt),pθ​(rt∣zt,at)),\displaystyle p_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid z_{t}),\,p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t})),

where eθe_{\theta} maps observation histories to latent states, pθ​(zt+1∣zt,at)p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t}) is the latent transition model, pθ​(ot∣zt)p_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid z_{t}) is the observation reconstruction or prediction model, and pθ​(rt∣zt,at)p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t}) is the reward prediction model.

Given a trajectory

τ=(o1,a1,r1,o2,a2,r2,…,oT),\tau=(o_{1},a_{1},r_{1},o_{2},a_{2},r_{2},\ldots,o_{T}), (B.4)

the latent world model induces the following factorization:

pθ(o1:T,r1:T,z1:T∣a1:T)=pθ(z1∣o1)\displaystyle p_{\theta}(o_{1:T},r_{1:T},z_{1:T}\mid a_{1:T})=p_{\theta}(z_{1}\mid o_{1}) (B.5)
×∏t=1Tpθ​(ot∣zt)​pθ​(rt∣zt,at)​pθ​(zt+1∣zt,at).\displaystyle\times\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid z_{t})p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t})p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t}).

This factorization shows that the model compresses the observable history into latent states while preserving the information needed to predict future observations and rewards.

The learning objective is to fit the latent world model to trajectories collected from the environment. A common training objective is the negative log-likelihood

ℒWM(θ)=−∑t=1T[logpθ(ot∣zt)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WM}}(\theta)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big[\log p_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid z_{t}) (B.6)
+logpθ(rt∣zt,at)+logpθ(zt+1∣zt,at)],\displaystyle+\log p_{\theta}(r_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t})+\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t})\Big],

where zt=eθ​(ht)z_{t}=e_{\theta}(h_{t}). In variational latent world models, the latent transition term can be replaced by an evidence lower bound that includes an inference model qθ​(zt∣ht)q_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid h_{t}) and a prior transition model pθ​(zt∣zt−1,at−1)p_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1}).

After training, the latent world model can be used for multi-step imagination or planning. Starting from an inferred latent state ztz_{t}, the model recursively predicts future latent states under a candidate action sequence (at,at+1,…,at+H−1)(a_{t},a_{t+1},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}):

z^t+k+1∼pθ​(z^t+k+1∣z^t+k,at+k),\hat{z}_{t+k+1}\sim p_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k+1}\mid\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k}), (B.7)

k=0,1,…,H−1k=0,1,\ldots,H-1, with z^t=zt\hat{z}_{t}=z_{t}. The predicted return of this imagined trajectory is

J^θ(at:t+H−1∣zt)=𝔼𝒲θ[∑k=0H−1γkr^t+k],\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{W}_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\hat{r}_{t+k}\right], (B.8)

where

r^t+k∼pθ​(r^t+k∣z^t+k,at+k).\hat{r}_{t+k}\sim p_{\theta}(\hat{r}_{t+k}\mid\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k}). (B.9)

The planning problem can then be written as

at:t+H−1⋆=argmaxat:t+H−1J^θ(at:t+H−1∣zt).a_{t:t+H-1}^{\star}=\arg\max_{a_{t:t+H-1}}\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t}). (B.10)

Thus, a latent world model is an action-conditioned predictive representation of the environment. It learns a latent state space in which the agent can simulate future trajectories, estimate their rewards, and select actions according to predicted long-term outcomes.

B.2 Error Propagation in Latent World Models

We first study how a one-step latent transition error propagates through multi-step imagination. We consider the deterministic mean dynamics induced by the latent world model. Let

z^t+1=Fθ​(z^t,at)\hat{z}_{t+1}=F_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t},a_{t}) (B.11)

denote the learned latent transition, and let

zt+1=F⋆​(zt,at)z_{t+1}=F^{\star}(z_{t},a_{t}) (B.12)

denote the latent dynamics induced by the true environment under the same latent representation. Here, F⋆F^{\star} is not required to be a physical-state transition; it is the true transition map in the latent space.

Assumption 8 (Uniform one-step latent transition error).

There exists a constant ϵF≥0\epsilon_{F}\geq 0 such that

supz∈𝒵,a∈𝒜‖Fθ​(z,a)−F⋆​(z,a)‖≤ϵF.\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z},a\in\mathcal{A}}\left\|F_{\theta}(z,a)-F^{\star}(z,a)\right\|\leq\epsilon_{F}. (B.13)
Assumption 9 (Lipschitz continuity of the learned latent transition).

There exists a constant LF≥0L_{F}\geq 0 such that, for any z,z′∈𝒵z,z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A},

‖Fθ​(z,a)−Fθ​(z′,a)‖≤LF​‖z−z′‖.\left\|F_{\theta}(z,a)-F_{\theta}(z^{\prime},a)\right\|\leq L_{F}\left\|z-z^{\prime}\right\|. (B.14)

Given an action sequence at:t+H−1a_{t:t+H-1}, define the true latent rollout and the imagined latent rollout as

zt+k+1\displaystyle z_{t+k+1} =F⋆​(zt+k,at+k),\displaystyle=F^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k}), (B.15)
z^t+k+1\displaystyle\hat{z}_{t+k+1} =Fθ​(z^t+k,at+k),\displaystyle=F_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k}),

for k=0,1,…,H−1k=0,1,\ldots,H-1. Define the kk-step rollout error by

ek=‖z^t+k−zt+k‖.e_{k}=\left\|\hat{z}_{t+k}-z_{t+k}\right\|. (B.16)
Theorem 6 (Multi-step latent transition error propagation).

Suppose Assumptions 8 and 9 hold. Then, for any fixed action sequence at:t+H−1a_{t:t+H-1} and any k=0,1,…,Hk=0,1,\ldots,H,

ek\displaystyle e_{k} ≤LFk​e0+ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi.\displaystyle\leq L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}. (B.17)

Equivalently, if LF≠1L_{F}\neq 1,

ek\displaystyle e_{k} ≤LFk​e0+ϵF​LFk−1LF−1\displaystyle\leq L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\frac{L_{F}^{k}-1}{L_{F}-1} (B.18)
=O⁡(LFk​e0+ϵF​LFk).\displaystyle=O(L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}L_{F}^{k}).

If LF=1L_{F}=1, then ek≤e0+k​ϵF=O⁡(e0+k​ϵF)e_{k}\leq e_{0}+k\epsilon_{F}=O(e_{0}+k\epsilon_{F}). In particular, if the initial latent state is exact, namely e0=0e_{0}=0, then

ek≤ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi={O⁡(ϵF),0≤LF<1,O⁡(k​ϵF),LF=1,O⁡(ϵF​LFk),LF>1.e_{k}\leq\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}=\begin{cases}O(\epsilon_{F}),&0\leq L_{F}<1,\\ O(k\epsilon_{F}),&L_{F}=1,\\ O(\epsilon_{F}L_{F}^{k}),&L_{F}>1.\end{cases} (B.19)
Proof.

For each k=0,1,…,H−1k=0,1,\ldots,H-1, we have

ek+1=‖Fθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−F⋆​(zt+k,at+k)‖.e_{k+1}=\left\|F_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-F^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right\|. (B.20)

Adding and subtracting Fθ​(zt+k,at+k)F_{\theta}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k}) gives

ek+1≤‖Fθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−Fθ​(zt+k,at+k)‖\displaystyle e_{k+1}\leq\left\|F_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-F_{\theta}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right\| (B.21)
+‖Fθ​(zt+k,at+k)−F⋆​(zt+k,at+k)‖.\displaystyle+\left\|F_{\theta}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})-F^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right\|. (B.22)

By Assumption 9, the first term is bounded by

LF​‖z^t+k−zt+k‖=LF​ek.L_{F}\left\|\hat{z}_{t+k}-z_{t+k}\right\|=L_{F}e_{k}. (B.23)

By Assumption 8, the second term is bounded by ϵF\epsilon_{F}. Therefore,

ek+1≤LF​ek+ϵF.e_{k+1}\leq L_{F}e_{k}+\epsilon_{F}. (B.24)

Unrolling this recursion of Equation (B.24) yields

ek≤LFk​e0+ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi.e_{k}\leq L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}. (B.25)

When LF≠1L_{F}\neq 1, the geometric sum satisfies

∑i=0k−1LFi=LFk−1LF−1.\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}=\frac{L_{F}^{k}-1}{L_{F}-1}. (B.26)

When LF=1L_{F}=1, the recursion becomes ek+1≤ek+ϵFe_{k+1}\leq e_{k}+\epsilon_{F}, and hence ek≤e0+k​ϵFe_{k}\leq e_{0}+k\epsilon_{F}. ∎

Theorem 6 shows that even a uniformly bounded one-step transition error can increase across a multi-step imagined trajectory. When LF<1L_{F}<1, the transition is contractive and the accumulated error remains controlled. When LF=1L_{F}=1, the error grows at most linearly in the planning horizon. When LF>1L_{F}>1, the error bound grows geometrically, which gives a formal explanation of compounding error in latent world models.

B.3 Reward Prediction and Return Error Bound

We next show that latent transition error induces reward prediction error and therefore biases the planning objective. Let the learned reward model be

r^t+k=Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k),\hat{r}_{t+k}=R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k}), (B.27)

and let the true latent reward function be

rt+k=R⋆​(zt+k,at+k).r_{t+k}=R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k}). (B.28)

For a fixed horizon HH, define the learned imagined return and the true return under the same action sequence as

J^θ(at:t+H−1∣z^t)=∑k=0H−1γkRθ(z^t+k,at+k)\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid\hat{z}_{t})=\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k}) (B.29)

and

J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)=∑k=0H−1γkR⋆(zt+k,at+k).J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})=\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k}). (B.30)
Assumption 10 (Uniform one-step reward model error).

There exists a constant ϵR≥0\epsilon_{R}\geq 0 such that

supz∈𝒵,a∈𝒜|Rθ​(z,a)−R⋆​(z,a)|≤ϵR.\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z},a\in\mathcal{A}}\left|R_{\theta}(z,a)-R^{\star}(z,a)\right|\leq\epsilon_{R}. (B.31)

The previous theorem bounds the deviation of the imagined latent trajectory from the true latent trajectory. We now show that this latent rollout error directly induces reward prediction error, because the reward model is evaluated on the imagined latent states rather than on the true latent states.

Assumption 11 (Lipschitz continuity of the learned reward model).

There exists a constant LR≥0L_{R}\geq 0 such that, for any z,z′∈𝒵z,z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A},

|Rθ​(z,a)−Rθ​(z′,a)|≤LR​‖z−z′‖.\left|R_{\theta}(z,a)-R_{\theta}(z^{\prime},a)\right|\leq L_{R}\left\|z-z^{\prime}\right\|. (B.32)
Proposition 7 (Reward prediction error bound).

Suppose Assumptions 8, 9, 10, and 11 hold. For any fixed action sequence at:t+H−1a_{t:t+H-1} and any k=0,1,…,H−1k=0,1,\ldots,H-1, define

ΔkR=|Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−R⋆​(zt+k,at+k)|.\Delta^{R}_{k}=\left|R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right|. (B.33)

Then

ΔkR≤LR​(LFk​e0+ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi)+ϵR.\displaystyle\Delta^{R}_{k}\leq L_{R}\left(L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}\right)+\epsilon_{R}. (B.34)

In particular, if e0=0e_{0}=0, then

ΔkR≤LR​ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi+ϵR.\Delta^{R}_{k}\leq L_{R}\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}+\epsilon_{R}. (B.35)

Proposition 7 separates the reward prediction error into two sources. The first term comes from latent state mismatch and scales with the transition error accumulated through the rollout. The second term, ϵR\epsilon_{R}, is the intrinsic one-step approximation error of the reward model. Therefore, even when the reward model is uniformly accurate at one step, the reward estimate can still degrade over a long imagined trajectory because the latent inputs themselves become increasingly biased.

Proof.

For any k=0,1,…,H−1k=0,1,\ldots,H-1, adding and subtracting Rθ​(zt+k,at+k)R_{\theta}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k}) gives

|Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−R⋆​(zt+k,at+k)|\displaystyle\left|R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right|
≤|Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−Rθ​(zt+k,at+k)|\displaystyle\leq\left|R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R_{\theta}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right|
+|Rθ​(zt+k,at+k)−R⋆​(zt+k,at+k)|.\displaystyle+\left|R_{\theta}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right|. (B.36)

By Assumption 11, the first term is bounded by

LR​‖z^t+k−zt+k‖=LR​ek.L_{R}\left\|\hat{z}_{t+k}-z_{t+k}\right\|=L_{R}e_{k}. (B.37)

By Assumption 10, the second term is bounded by ϵR\epsilon_{R}. Thus,

|Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−R⋆​(zt+k,at+k)|≤LR​ek+ϵR.\left|R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right|\leq L_{R}e_{k}+\epsilon_{R}. (B.38)

Applying Theorem 6 gives

ek≤LFk​e0+ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi.e_{k}\leq L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}. (B.39)

Substituting this bound into the reward error inequality proves the result. ∎

Proposition 8 (Multi-step return error bound).

Suppose Assumptions 8, 9, 10, and 11 hold. Then, for any fixed action sequence at:t+H−1a_{t:t+H-1},

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣z^t)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid\hat{z}_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.40)
≤∑k=0H−1γk​[LR​(LFk​e0+ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi)+ϵR].\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\left[L_{R}\left(L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}\right)+\epsilon_{R}\right]. (B.41)

If the initial latent state is exact, namely e0=0e_{0}=0, then

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣zt)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.42)
≤∑k=0H−1γk​(LR​ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi+ϵR).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\left(L_{R}\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}+\epsilon_{R}\right).

Furthermore, when e0=0e_{0}=0, LF=1L_{F}=1, and γ=1\gamma=1, the return error satisfies

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣zt)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.43)
≤LR​ϵF​H​(H−1)2+ϵR​H.\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{R}\epsilon_{F}H(H-1)}{2}+\epsilon_{R}H. (B.44)

Consequently,

|J^θ−J⋆|=O⁡(LR​ϵF​H2+ϵR​H).\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}-J^{\star}\right|=O(L_{R}\epsilon_{F}H^{2}+\epsilon_{R}H). (B.45)

Proposition 8 shows that transition error affects planning through the cumulative return objective. When e0=0e_{0}=0, LF=1L_{F}=1, and γ=1\gamma=1, the return error scales as O⁡(LR​ϵF​H2+ϵR​H)O(L_{R}\epsilon_{F}H^{2}+\epsilon_{R}H). Thus, a one-step latent transition error of order ϵF\epsilon_{F} can lead to a quadratic dependence on the planning horizon, while the reward approximation error accumulates linearly. This explains why a latent world model with small one-step prediction error may still produce biased long-horizon planning estimates.

Proof.

By definition,

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣z^t)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid\hat{z}_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.46)
=|∑k=0H−1γk​[Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−R⋆​(zt+k,at+k)]|.\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\left[R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right]\right|. (B.47)

Using the triangle inequality,

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣z^t)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid\hat{z}_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right|
≤∑k=0H−1γk​|Rθ​(z^t+k,at+k)−R⋆​(zt+k,at+k)|.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\left|R_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k})-R^{\star}(z_{t+k},a_{t+k})\right|. (B.48)

Applying Proposition 7 to each summand yields

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣z^t)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid\hat{z}_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.49)
≤∑k=0H−1γk​[LR​(LFk​e0+ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi)+ϵR].\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\left[L_{R}\left(L_{F}^{k}e_{0}+\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}\right)+\epsilon_{R}\right]. (B.50)

If e0=0e_{0}=0, this reduces to

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣zt)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.51)
≤∑k=0H−1γk​(LR​ϵF​∑i=0k−1LFi+ϵR).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\left(L_{R}\epsilon_{F}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}+\epsilon_{R}\right). (B.52)

When LF=1L_{F}=1, we have ∑i=0k−1LFi=k\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}L_{F}^{i}=k. When also γ=1\gamma=1, the bound becomes

∑k=0H−1(LR​ϵF​k+ϵR)=LR​ϵF​∑k=0H−1k+ϵR​H.\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\left(L_{R}\epsilon_{F}k+\epsilon_{R}\right)=L_{R}\epsilon_{F}\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}k+\epsilon_{R}H. (B.53)

Since ∑k=0H−1k=H⁡(H−1)2\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}k=\frac{H(H-1)}{2}, we obtain

|J^θ(at:t+H−1∣zt)−J⋆(at:t+H−1∣zt)|\displaystyle\left|\hat{J}_{\theta}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})-J^{\star}(a_{t:t+H-1}\mid z_{t})\right| (B.54)
≤LR​ϵF​H​(H−1)2+ϵR​H.\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{R}\epsilon_{F}H(H-1)}{2}+\epsilon_{R}H. (B.55)

This proves the stated asymptotic rate. ∎
